sourceIssues.locator: §4, proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4, paragraph beginning "On the other side of characteristic l′" (checking the hypothesis of Lemma 2.1 at λ′), p. 1270; uses Lemma 3.9 and formulas (3.1)–(3.3), pp. 1262–1264
sourceIssues.printed: The source states det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′} = (χ_cyc)^{n(n−1)/2} with image in F^×_{l^2}. Applying Lemma 3.9 at l′, it concludes that (det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′})^∨ ⊗ (det V[λ′]), regarded as a G_{F(ζ_N)}-representation, has image in (k(λ′)^×)^n.
sourceIssues.correction: Prove the step from the Frobenius computation inside the proof of Lemma 3.9, not from the statement of the lemma. Let v be a place of F(ζ_N) not dividing Nll′, and let q = #k(v). By (3.1), det V[λ′](Frob_v) = (q^{(N−3)/2} ∏_j g(v,b_j))^n · q^{−n(n−1)/2}. For geometric Frobenius on H^1, det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′}(Frob_v) = q^{n(n−1)/2}. So (det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′})^∨ ⊗ det V[λ′] sends Frob_v to (q^{(N−2n−1)/2} ∏_j g(v,b_j))^n. The exponent (N−2n−1)/2 is an integer because N is odd. By (3.2)–(3.3), ∏_j g(v,b_j) lies in Q(ζ_N) (in Q(ζ_N)^+ when n = 2) and is a unit at λ′, so the base reduces into k(λ′)^× = F_{l′}^×. By Chebotarev, the character takes values in (k(λ′)^×)^n. With the paper's own sign for det Symm^{n−1}, the value is instead (q^{(N−3)/2} ∏_j g(v,b_j))^n, which is also an n-th power. The clause "which have image in F^×_{l^2}" should refer to l′, not l: the character takes values in F_{l′}^×, and for even n those values are in general n-th powers only in F_{l′^2}^×.
sourceIssues.reason: Lemma 3.9 at λ′ gives only det V[λ′](G_F) ⊂ (F_{l′^2}^× k(λ′)^×)^n. Here k(λ′) = F_{l′} because l′ ≡ 1 mod N. On the l side the paper imposed F_{l^2} ⊂ k(λ), but no such condition is available at λ′. Knowing that an element of F_{l′}^× is an n-th power in F_{l′^2}^× does not make it an n-th power in F_{l′}^×. For example, every element of F_{l′}^× is a square in F_{l′^2}. The two determinants also cannot be treated one at a time. Take n even with n | l′−1, as Lemma 2.1 needs. The character χ̄_cyc is onto F_{l′}^× on G_{F(ζ_N)}, because F(ζ_N) is unramified at l′. So there are places v with q a non-square mod l′. At such a v, det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′}(Frob_v) = q^{±n(n−1)/2} is not an n-th power in F_{l′}^×, and so det V[λ′](Frob_v) is not one either. Only their quotient is an n-th power, because the half-integral powers of q cancel as in (3.1). The paper never states this cancellation. When n is odd, the proof of Lemma 3.9 already gives n-th powers in k(λ′)^×, so the gap concerns even n only. The conclusion is true and the stated theorems are unaffected. I checked this numerically with Gauss sums reduced modulo a prime over l′, at a degree-one place with q = p ≡ 1 mod N a non-residue mod l′, for: N = 503, n = 2 (q = 15091, l′ = 15181547); N = 503, n = 4 (q = 3019, l′ = 6037); N = 505, n = 6 (q = 5051, l′ = 76522651); N = 503, n = 8 (q = 3019, l′ = 54674089). In every case (3.1) holds and ∏_j g(v,b_j) reduces into F_{l′}. Neither det V[λ′](Frob_v) nor q^{n(n−1)/2} is an n-th power in F_{l′}^×, while their quotient is one and equals (q^{(N−2n−1)/2} ∏_j g(v,b_j))^n. For n = 3 (q = 3019, l′ = 45556711), both factors are cubes.

sourceIssues.locator: §4, proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4: Lemma 2.1 is applied at the auxiliary prime λ′ in the paragraph beginning "Now, apply Lemma 2.1" and the paragraph beginning "On the other side of characteristic l′", p. 1270. The hypothesis of Lemma 2.1 is on p. 1244, and the choice of l′ is in Proposition 4.1, p. 1269.
sourceIssues.printed: The source asserts that the condition required by Lemma 2.1 is checked in the subsequent argument.
sourceIssues.correction:
Add the condition l′ ≡ 1 mod n to Proposition 4.1, so that l′ ≡ 1 mod Nn (N and n are coprime). These primes have Dirichlet density 1/φ(Nn) > 0. The other conditions on l′ exclude only a finite set or a set of density 0, and the fourth condition still follows from the second and third. The later uses of l′ impose no congruence condition that could conflict: the Section 3 hypotheses, Proposition 3.8, and the first paragraph of the proof of ACC+ Corollary 7.2.4. With this condition, k(λ′) = F_{l′} contains μ_n and Lemma 2.1 applies as stated.

Alternatively, the gap closes without any new condition on l′. Put d = gcd(n, l′−1). Then (F_{l′}^×)^n = (F_{l′}^×)^d, and F_{l′} contains μ_d, so Lemma 2.1 with exponent d gives ψ_0 with ψ_0^d = χ. Build an n-th root ψ of χ one primary component of the cyclic group F_{l′}^× at a time:
- if v_p(n) ≤ v_p(l′−1), then n/d is prime to p, and the p-part of ψ is the p-part of ψ_0 raised to an inverse of n/d modulo p^{v_p(l′−1)};
- if v_p(n) > v_p(l′−1), then the p-part of χ is trivial, and so is the p-part of ψ.
Equivalently, the proof of Lemma 2.1 goes through with Z/mZ replaced by μ_n(F_{l^r}), which is cyclic of order gcd(m, l^r−1).
sourceIssues.reason:
Lemma 2.1 (p. 1244) assumes that the finite field F_{l^r} contains all n-th roots of unity. Its proof uses this to identify the kernel of x ↦ x^n on F_{l^r}^× with Z/mZ, where n = l^a m.

In §4 (p. 1270) the lemma is used to produce two characters: χ_1 valued in k(λ)^× and χ_2 valued in k(λ′)^×. For λ the paper states that n | #(k(λ)^×); this comes from the choice of N, up to replacing n by m. For λ′ nothing corresponding is said, and the paragraph on λ′ checks only that the determinant quotient takes values in (k(λ′)^×)^n.

Since l′ ≡ 1 mod N, the prime l′ splits completely in Q(ζ_N), and also in Q(ζ_N)^+ when n = 2, so k(λ′) = F_{l′}. Since l′ > 2ln + 5 > n, F_{l′} contains μ_n exactly when n | l′−1. Proposition 4.1 (p. 1269) imposes only l′ ≡ 1 mod N. Because gcd(N, n) = 1, this says nothing about l′ modulo n. So the hypothesis of Lemma 2.1 is not verified, and it can fail whenever n ≥ 3; for n = 2 it holds automatically.

Small cases:
- n = 3, N = 401 (odd, prime to 3l for l ≠ 401, and greater than 100n + 100). The least prime l′ ≡ 1 mod 401 is 3209, which is 2 mod 3, so F_3209 has no primitive cube root of unity.
- n = 4, N = 503. The least prime l′ ≡ 1 mod 503 is 3019, which is 3 mod 4, so μ_4(F_3019) = {±1}.
In both cases Lemma 2.1 does not apply as stated, but the required root still exists. Cubing is bijective on F_3209^×. In the second case the fourth powers equal the squares, a group of odd order on which the fourth-power map is bijective.

In general the conclusion of Lemma 2.1 holds for every finite field. Both repairs above are valid, and either is sufficient for this point. So this is a missing verification in the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.4, which share this construction; neither theorem is affected. A separate question is whether the determinant quotient at λ′ really lands in (k(λ′)^×)^n. That is not addressed by this repair and is recorded separately.

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 3.11, statement (1) and proof of (2) and (3), p. 1267
sourceIssues.printed: The source asserts that V_{λ,t} is de Rham as a G_F-representation. It derives (2) from good reduction of Y_t over the residue field of F and, for (3), uses t ∈ 𝔪_F to assert (V_{λ,0} ⊗_{τ,F} B_cris)^{Gal(F̄/F)} ≅ (V_{λ,t} ⊗_{τ,F} B_cris)^{Gal(F̄/F)}.
sourceIssues.correction: Replace F with F_v throughout. Read “a de Rham representation of G_{F_v}”, “the maximal ideal of O_{F_v}” and “t ∈ 𝔪_{F_v}”. Take the invariants in the displayed isomorphism under Gal(F̄_v/F_v). By Remark 2.5 (p. 1251), the display is D_{cris,τ}(V_{λ,0}) ≅ D_{cris,τ}(V_{λ,t}), so the tensor product is taken over the maximal unramified subfield: ⊗_{τ,F_v^0} B_cris. Reading ⊗_{τ,F_v} would fail when F_v/ℚ_l is ramified, because B_cris is not an F_v-algebra in that case.
sourceIssues.reason:
The page image matches the recorded text exactly, so this is not a text-layer artefact. On p. 1266, v is a place of the number field F above l, and the lemma takes t ∈ F_v as a point of T_0(F_v). So V_{λ,t} is the fibre of the lisse sheaf V_λ at a local point, which makes it a representation of G_{F_v}. It need not come from a representation of G_F.

The rest of the lemma is written locally. The embeddings in (1) are σ : F_v ↪ \overline{ℚ(ζ_N)_λ}, and the hypotheses of (2) and (3) are stated with O_{F_v} and 𝔪_{F_v}. Lemma 3.12, on the same page, explicitly treats V_{λ′,t} as a G_{F_v}-representation. A number field F has no maximal ideal in the sense needed for good reduction, and t ∈ 𝔪_F makes no sense for t ∈ F_v.

The slip comes from a partial change of notation. In arXiv v1 (p. 19), F denotes a finite extension of ℚ(ζ_N)_v, which is a local field. There the corresponding lemma (Lemma 3.10, p. 20) consistently writes G_F, O_F, 𝔪_F and ⊗_{σ,F} B_cris. The published version renamed this local field F_v but did not carry the change through the lemma.

The displayed module in the proof of (3) is the D_{cris,τ} of Remark 2.5. It feeds into Lemma 2.4, which is stated with ⊗_{τ,F_v^0} B_cris, so F_v^0 is the right subscript for the tensor product. The meaning is clear from the statement and the surrounding text, and nothing depends on the slip.

sourceIssues.locator: Section 4, proof of Theorem 1.1, the paragraph after Proposition 4.1 that begins "On the other side of characteristic l′", p. 1270. The same sentence appears unchanged in arXiv v1, p. 22. The representation r̄_{E,l′} is defined in the opening paragraph of Section 4, on p. 1268.
sourceIssues.printed: The source gives det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′} = (χ_cyc)^{n(n−1)/2} and says its image lies in F_{l′²}^×.
sourceIssues.correction: det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′} = χ̄_cyc^{−n(n−1)/2}, where χ̄_cyc is the mod-l′ cyclotomic character. The paper defines r̄_{E,l′} as H^1_ét(E, F_{l′}) (p. 1268). The printed formula holds instead for the l′-torsion E[l′], that is, for the Tate-module convention. In that convention r_{E,l} is the Tate module and the automorphic object is its dual, as in ACC+, Corollary 7.2.4. The rest of the argument is unchanged, because both characters take values in F_{l′}^× ⊂ F_{l′²}^×.
sourceIssues.reason: By the Weil pairing, ∧²E[l′] ≅ μ_{l′}, so det E[l′] = χ̄_cyc. H^1_ét(E_{Q̄}, F_{l′}) is the F_{l′}-dual of E[l′], so its determinant is χ̄_cyc^{−1}. The same follows from Frobenius eigenvalues. At a prime p ≠ l′ of good reduction, geometric Frobenius acts on H^1 with eigenvalues α, β, where αβ = p. The paper uses χ_cyc in the standard sense (compare the central-character identity on p. 1273), so χ_cyc sends geometric Frobenius to p^{−1}. Now take any 2-dimensional representation whose Frobenius eigenvalues are a and b. The eigenvalues on Symm^{n−1} are a^{n−1−i}b^i for 0 ≤ i ≤ n−1, whose product is (ab)^{n(n−1)/2}. Hence det Symm^{n−1} r̄_{E,l′} = χ̄_cyc^{−n(n−1)/2}. The printed identity is false in general. For n = 2 it would say det r̄_{E,l′} = χ̄_cyc, whereas the true determinant is χ̄_cyc^{−1}. These differ by χ̄_cyc², which is nontrivial on G_{F(ζ_N)}: there l′ > 5 and l′ is unramified in F(ζ_N), so χ̄_cyc maps G_{F(ζ_N)} onto F_{l′}^×. The slip is harmless, and its intended meaning is clear. The next sentence uses only that this determinant is a power of the mod-l′ cyclotomic character, so that its values lie in F_{l′}^× ⊂ F_{l′²}^×, and that holds for either sign. Moreover, the two candidates differ by χ̄_cyc^{n(n−1)} = (χ̄_cyc^{n−1})^n, an n-th power. So the n-th-power statement drawn from it with Lemma 3.9 does not depend on the sign. The paper's H^1 convention is itself consistent with the automorphy input in Proposition 4.1: ACC+, Corollary 7.2.4 proves automorphy of the dual of Symm^m of the Tate module, which is Symm^m H^1. The exponent n(n−1)/2 appears to have been carried over from the Tate-module convention; the introduction (p. 1244) also speaks of "the Tate module of an elliptic curve". Since the paper fixes both r̄_{E,l′} and χ_cyc explicitly, the sign is not a matter of convention within the paper.

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 4.2 of L. Qian, "Ordinarity of local Galois representation arising from Dwork motives", arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 20. This preprint is reference [14] of the paper and exists only in this version. The paper does not cite Lemma 4.2. It refers only to the main theorem of [14], in Remark 3.13 (p. 1267) and Remark 4.4 (p. 1273). Lemma 3.12 (p. 1266) does not cite [14]. In arXiv v1 of the paper, Lemma 3.10(4) (v1, pp. 20–21) was proved as "the main theorem of [Qia21]". The published version dropped that part.
sourceIssues.printed: Lemma 4.2 takes a characteristic 0 local field F_v over ℚ_p and semistable r : Gal(F̄_v/F_v) → GL_n(ℚ̄_p). For every τ : F_v^0 ↪ ℚ̄_p, it assumes that N on (r ⊗_{τ,F_v^0} B_st)^{Gal(F̄_v/F_v)}, of dimension n, has smallest vanishing power N^j = 0 at j = n. It concludes that r is regular and ordinary, attributing the assertion to Lemma 2.2 (2) of [BLGHT09].
sourceIssues.correction:
Add the Hodge–Tate hypothesis of BLGHT Lemma 2.2(2), in shifted form: for every embedding τ : F_v ↪ ℚ̄_p there is an integer k_τ such that the τ-labelled Hodge–Tate weights of r are k_τ, k_τ+1, …, k_τ+n−1, each with multiplicity one. Then r is regular and ordinary.

The case k_τ = 0 is exactly BLGHT Lemma 2.2(2), with conclusion "ordinary of weight 0". The general case follows by twisting by a crystalline character with τ-labelled weight −k_τ; the twist changes neither semistability nor N. It also follows directly from the same weak-admissibility argument.

The proof of the preprint's Theorem 1.1 must then check this hypothesis for V_{λ,t^{-1}}. It holds: the theorem assumes maximally unipotent monodromy at ∞ for every conjugate σχ, and this forces the Hodge numbers of each eigenpart to be 1 in n consecutive degrees.
sourceIssues.reason:
Lemma 4.2 omits a hypothesis of the result it quotes. BLGHT Lemma 2.2(2) also assumes that for every τ the τ-labelled Hodge–Tate weights are exactly 0, 1, …, n−1, each with multiplicity one. Without that hypothesis the statement is false already for n = 2 over ℚ_p.

Counterexample. Let D have basis e1, e2 with φ(e1) = p·e1, φ(e2) = p²·e2, N(e2) = e1 and N(e1) = 0. Then Nφ(e2) = p²·e1 = pφN(e2), so Nφ = pφN. Give D the filtration Fil⁰ = D, Fil¹ = Fil² = Fil³ = ⟨e1+e2⟩, Fil⁴ = 0.
- t_H(D) = 0 + 3 = 3, and t_N(D) = v_p(p·p²) = 3.
- The only nonzero proper N-stable subspace is ker N = ⟨e1⟩. There t_H = 0 ≤ 1 = t_N.
- So D is weakly admissible. By Colmez–Fontaine it is D_st(V) for a 2-dimensional semistable V with Hodge–Tate weights {0, 3} and N ≠ 0, so N is maximally nilpotent and V is regular.
- A G_{ℚ_p}-stable line in V would give a (φ,N)-stable line in D, or a rank-one quotient, with t_H = t_N. The only candidates are ⟨e1⟩ (t_H = 0, t_N = 1) and D/⟨e1⟩ (t_H = 3, t_N = 2).
- Hence V is irreducible and not ordinary, although it satisfies every hypothesis of Lemma 4.2.

Why the weights matter. When N is maximally nilpotent, the only (φ,N)-stable flag is ker N ⊂ ker N² ⊂ …. Because N maps each graded piece isomorphically onto the previous one and Nφ = pφN, the φ-slopes of the graded pieces are s, s+1, …, s+n−1. An ordinary flag needs rank-one admissible pieces, so ordinarity forces the labelled weights to be consecutive. Conversely, if the labelled weights are k_τ, …, k_τ+n−1, then t_H(D) = t_N(D) fixes s. Weak admissibility then forces each ker N^j to carry the lowest j weights at every τ and to be admissible. This gives the ordinary flag.

How far the error reaches.
- The false stated result is Lemma 4.2 itself.
- The preprint's proof of its Theorem 1.1 (pp. 20–23) applies Lemma 4.2 without ever computing Hodge–Tate weights, so that proof has a gap. The gap can be filled. In the limiting mixed Hodge structure at ∞, N has type (−1,−1) and commutes with H_0. Take v in a suitable Deligne component I^{p,q} of the χ-eigenspace. Then v, Nv, …, N^{n−1}v span that eigenspace, so its Hodge numbers are 1 in the n consecutive degrees p, p−1, …, p−n+1. By the de Rham comparison, and because the hypothesis holds for every σχ, these are the labelled Hodge–Tate weights. So Theorem 1.1 itself survives.
- For the family chosen in the paper, the consecutive weights are proved directly in Lemma 3.10(2) and Lemma 3.11(1) (pp. 1265–1266).
- The published paper uses neither Lemma 4.2 nor the main theorem of [14]. It gets ordinarity at l for v(t) < 0 from Lemma 4.3 (p. 1272), through Varma's local-global compatibility and Steinberg local components. Remark 3.13 (p. 1267) says the full strength of the main result of [14] is not needed.
- arXiv v1 of the paper used that main theorem in Lemma 3.10(4), where the consecutive weights were available from Lemma 3.10(1).
- So no stated result of the paper is affected.

sourceIssues.locator: Proposition 3.2, proof, first sentence, p. 1257
sourceIssues.printed: The source infers local freeness from smoothness and properness of the family.
sourceIssues.correction:
Smoothness and properness give only that the sheaves are locally constant. For V_λ and V[𝔫] this comes from smooth proper base change, and for V_B and V′_B from Ehresmann's theorem. Because the bases are connected, every stalk is then isomorphic to the stalk at one complex point, using the comparison with V_B stated just before the proposition. Local freeness needs three further facts.
(i) The integral cohomology of a smooth hypersurface Y_t ⊂ ℙ^{N−1} is torsion-free, by the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem and Poincaré duality. So H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ[ζ_N]) = H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ) ⊗ ℤ[ζ_N] is free. By the universal coefficient theorem, H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ[ζ_N]_λ) and H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ[ζ_N]/𝔫) are obtained from H^{N−2}(Y_t, ℤ) by tensoring, and they are also free.
(ii) For V_λ and V[𝔫], #H_0 = N^{N−2} is invertible in ℤ[ζ_N]_λ and in ℤ[ζ_N]/𝔫. So the χ-eigenpart is the image of an idempotent. It is a direct summand of a free module over a local ring, or over a finite product of local rings, and is therefore free.
(iii) For V_B and V′_B, N is not inverted. The χ-eigenpart is then a finitely generated submodule of a free module over the Dedekind ring ℤ[ζ_N], hence projective, that is, locally free in the sense of commutative algebra.
In every case the rank equals the dimension over ℚ(ζ_N) of the χ-eigenspace at t = 0. By Deligne's Proposition I.7.4 this dimension is n.
This argument gives only projective stalks for V_B and V′_B, not stalks free over ℤ[ζ_N] itself. The paper uses only their completions at λ and their reductions V_{B,t}/λ and V_{B,t}/𝔫 for λ, 𝔫 prime to 2N, and these are free of rank n.
sourceIssues.reason:
The printed sentence cannot hold as stated. A smooth proper family gives locally constant higher direct images, but their stalks can have torsion: an Enriques surface has H²(X, ℤ) ≅ ℤ^10 ⊕ ℤ/2. So local freeness needs the fibres' integral cohomology to be torsion-free, and it needs the χ-eigenpart to be a direct summand or at least projective. The paper gives neither.
I tried to defend it and the defence fails. The second sentence of the proof checks only the fibre over 0 through Proposition I.7.4 of [7]. That result counts dimensions over a field of characteristic 0 and gives the rank, not freeness. The paper says it adapts the proof of Lemma 4.1 of [4], and that proof does get freeness at t = 0 over ℤ[ζ_N, 1/2N]. But it inverts 2N, so it does not cover V_B or V′_B, whose coefficient ring is ℤ[ζ_N]. Nothing else in the paper supplies torsion-freeness or a direct-summand argument. The companion preprint (arXiv:2103.00106v1, p. 2) also asserts local freeness only "by standard comparison results".
The missing facts are standard, so the conclusion is correct. Everything used later concerns localizations or reductions at primes prime to 2N, where the stalks are free of rank n. So the kind is gap, and nothing downstream is affected.

sourceIssues.locator: Paragraph after Proposition 3.2 (the case n = 2), p. 1257
sourceIssues.printed: The source uses locally constant V_λ, V[𝔫], V_B with coefficients ℤ[ζ_N]^+_λ, ℤ[ζ_N]^+/𝔫, ℤ[ζ_N]^+, respectively. It identifies V_λ ⊗_{ℤ[ζ_N]^+} ℤ[ζ_N], V[𝔫] ⊗_{ℤ[ζ_N]^+} ℤ[ζ_N], V_B ⊗_{ℤ[ζ_N]^+} ℤ[ζ_N] identify respectively with the cited source’s U_λ, U[𝔫], U_B.
sourceIssues.correction: For V_B, read coefficients ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+ and V_B ⊗_{ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+} ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N] ≅ U_B. Nothing changes for V_λ and V[𝔫]. Here λ is a prime and 𝔫 a nonzero ideal of ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+, so both are prime to 2N. Hence ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+_λ = ℤ[ζ_N]^+_λ and ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+/𝔫 = ℤ[ζ_N]^+/(𝔫 ∩ ℤ[ζ_N]^+).
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked this against the page image. The sentence is printed exactly as recorded and is not an artefact of the text layer. The meaning is clear: the paper means to use the sheaves of [4, §4] for n = 2.

In [4, §4] these sheaves are cut out by an idempotent e with the prefactor 1/(2#H_0), where #H_0 = N^{N−2}. So e only exists once 2N is inverted, and [4] defines V_B = [e]^* R^{N−2}π_* ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+. Its perfect alternating pairing takes values in ℤ[ζ_N, 1/(2N)]^+. U_B is the χ-summand of R^{N−2}π_* ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N], and the projection isomorphism V_B ⊗_{ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+} ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N] ≅ U_B is stated over these rings. So [4] gives no ℤ[ζ_N]^+-structure on V_B, and the printed ℤ[ζ_N]^+ misstates what [4] defines. By contrast, [4] defines V_λ and V[𝔫] only for primes λ and nonzero ideals 𝔫 of ℤ[1/(2N), ζ_N]^+. The paper uses the same convention on p. 1256, so those two coefficient rings are correct as printed.

No argument is affected. For n = 2, V_B is used only through V_B/λ and V_B/𝔫 with λ and 𝔫 prime to 2N: in Corollary 4.7 of [4] as quoted on p. 1257, in Lemma 3.7 and in Proposition 3.8. It is also used through the unipotence of monodromy at ∞ in Lemma 3.12, which does not depend on the coefficient ring. Proposition 3.2's claim that V_B is locally free over ℤ[ζ_N] concerns the case n > 2, where V_B is defined over ℤ[ζ_N] as χ-isotypic invariants.

The wording is identical in arXiv:2104.09761v1, p. 13. The published article is the final version, and no erratum is known.

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 3.3(2), proof, p. 1257 (argument concluded on p. 1258)
sourceIssues.printed: The source reduces the argument to proving that monodromy around 0 on R^{N−2}p_*ℂ has characteristic polynomial equal to a power of (X − 1).
sourceIssues.correction:
The reduction is invalid. It has to be replaced by an argument that finds the eigenvalues of ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) itself, not those of its N-th power. The semistable-model argument that follows is still valid, but it proves only that the monodromy of ρ_t around t = ∞ is unipotent.

To prove (2), identify V′_B ⊗ ℂ with a hypergeometric local system on ℙ^1 − {0, 1, ∞}. There are two ways to do this:
- as [4] does for its Lemma 4.3(3), by citing Katz (Another look at the Dwork family, Theorem 5.3, together with Exponential sums and differential equations, Theorem 8.4.11);
- through the Picard–Fuchs equation and Levelt's theorem, as in A'Campo (arXiv:2407.16481v1, Lemmas 2.4.5 and 2.5.4 and Proposition 2.5.7).

The second route describes only the pull-back to the t-line, so it determines V′_B only up to a twist by a character ψ of the deck group μ_N. The hypotheses of §3 make n prime to N, so no nonzero translate of {b_1, …, b_n} in ℤ/Nℤ equals the set itself. Hence the hypergeometric system is not isomorphic to any nontrivial twist of itself, its pull-back is irreducible, and the eigenvalues at 0 from part (1) force ψ = 1.

Let e_1, …, e_n be the entries of (a_1, …, a_N) that remain after one copy of each residue that occurs is removed. Then ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) is conjugate to the companion matrix of ∏_k (X − ζ_N^{±e_k}), where a single sign, the same for every k, is fixed by the conventions for characters and loops. For the exponents chosen in §3 the only repeated residue is 0, which occurs n + 1 times. So every e_k = 0, and ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) has characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^n and a single Jordan block. This also gives Corollary 3.5 directly.
sourceIssues.reason:
For T ≠ 0 the fibre of Z_0: T(X_1^N + ⋯ + X_N^N) = N X_1⋯X_N is Y_{1/T}. So Z_0 is the Dwork family Y of §3 in the coordinate T = 1/t, not the family Y′ over the t′-line, and its monodromy around T = 0 is the monodromy of ρ_t around t = ∞. The covering t ↦ t′ = t^N is totally ramified over t′ = ∞. A small loop around t = ∞ therefore maps to a conjugate of γ_∞^{±N}, and the pull-back of V′_B is V_B. The blow-up from Lemma 2.1 of [14] and the local monodromy theorem (reduced divisor, e = 1) thus prove only that ρ_{t′}(γ_∞)^N is unipotent, that is, that the eigenvalues of ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) are N-th roots of unity.

The argument never uses the exponents a_j, and for other characters of H_0 the conclusion it claims is false. Take N = 5 and (a_1, …, a_5) = (1, 2, 2, 0, 0). Then Σa_j ≡ 0, a_N = 0, {b_1, b_2} = {1, 2} and n = 2.
- The proof of (1) applies word for word and gives det ρ_{t′}(γ_0) = ζ_5^{±3} ≠ 1.
- The fibres over μ_N have only ordinary double points, and the fibre dimension N − 2 = 3 is odd. By Picard–Lefschetz, ρ_{t′}(γ_1) is unipotent.
- Since γ_0γ_1γ_∞ = 1, det ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) ≠ 1, so ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) is not unipotent, although the argument of (2) applies to this character word for word.

The same failure occurs for every odd N ≥ 5. Let (a_j) consist of each residue other than −b_1, …, −b_n once, together with n extra entries e_1, …, e_n that avoid the −b_j. Then Σb_j ≡ −Σe_k mod N and det ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) = ζ_N^{±Σe_k}. Any such choice with Σe_k ≢ 0 therefore breaks the argument; an example is b = {1, N − 3} with e = (1, 1).

No reading of the paper rescues the step. The deck-group action on the limit at t = ∞, which would supply the missing eigenvalues in the way part (1) does at t = 0, is never computed. The extra facts (1), (3) and det = 1 do not fix the eigenvalues at ∞ when n ≥ 2. Lemma 3.4 cannot help, because it takes (2) as input.

For the paper's exponents the nonzero entries are distinct and 0 occurs n + 1 times, so every e_k = 0. This is why the statement of Lemma 3.3(2) is still true although its proof fails. A'Campo's Proposition 2.5.7 agrees: on the t-line the monodromy at ∞ is a single unipotent Jordan block. For the counterexample character his parameters give eigenvalues 1 and ζ_5^{±3} at t′ = ∞.

The same step appears in arXiv:2104.09761v1, proof of Lemma 3.3(2), pp. 13–14. Part (2) is used for the eigenvalues at ∞ in Lemma 3.4, and hence in:
- Corollary 3.5;
- the l-power order of the reduction of ρ_{t′}(γ_∞) in the proof of Lemma 3.7 (p. 1259);
- det(γ_∞) = 1 on p. 1260;
- maximal unipotence at ∞ in Lemma 3.12 (p. 1268).
All of these stand once (2) is proved as in the correction. BLGHT's Lemma 4.3(3) had deferred exactly this point to Katz and wished for a direct argument. The printed direct argument does not supply one.

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 3.3(3), statement p. 1257; proof of (3), p. 1258
sourceIssues.printed: The source attributes the proof of (3) to the argument for [4], Lemma 4.3, part 2.
sourceIssues.correction:
Keep the Picard–Lefschetz half of the cited argument. The fibre over t′ = 1 has N^{N−2} ordinary double points, and H_0 permutes them simply transitively. So on the χ-part, ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1 has image in the line spanned by the χ-projection of a single vanishing cycle, and rank(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) ≤ 1.

Replace the symplectic step with either of the following arguments.

(a) Determinant. By (1), (2) and γ_0γ_1γ_∞ = 1, det ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = ζ_N^{−(b_1+⋯+b_n)}. Moreover b_1+⋯+b_n ≡ a_1+⋯+a_N ≡ 0 mod N, for three reasons:
- {b_1,…,b_n} is the complement of {−a_1,…,−a_N} in ℤ/Nℤ;
- the nonzero a_j are pairwise distinct;
- the elements of ℤ/Nℤ sum to 0 when N is odd.
This agrees with the explicit list of the b_j on p. 1254. Write ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = 1 + v ⊗ f. Then det ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = 1 + f(v) = 1, so f(v) = 0 and (ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1)^2 = f(v)(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) = 0. Hence ρ_{t′}(γ_1) is unipotent.

(b) Odd-dimensional Picard–Lefschetz. The fibres have odd dimension N − 2, so the cup product on H^{N−2} is alternating. The vanishing cycles are therefore isotropic, and they are pairwise orthogonal because the double points are distinct. Hence (γ_1 − 1)^2 = 0 on all of H^{N−2} of the fibre, and so also on its χ-part.

Finally, [4] gives only dim ker ≥ n − 1, so the exact equality dim ker(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) = n − 1 needs one more step. If ρ_{t′}(γ_1) = 1, then ρ_{t′}(γ_0) = ρ_{t′}(γ_∞)^{−1} would be unipotent. This contradicts (1), because no b_j is 0 in ℤ/Nℤ.
sourceIssues.reason:
The proof of [4, Lemma 4.3(2)] has two steps.
- Picard–Lefschetz theory shows that ker(γ_1 − 1) has rank at least n − 1. This part carries over unchanged to the family Y′ with the character χ.
- Unipotence then follows from the sentence "As γ_1 acts as a symplectic transformation we conclude that it has characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^n". This works in [4] because the χ-part there becomes, after extending scalars, the sheaf Ṽ_B, which carries a perfect alternating pairing, and ρ̃ takes values in Sp_n. In effect the step uses det = 1.

Neither step can be replaced by a symplectic structure in the present setting. The cup product pairs the χ-part of H^{N−2} only with the χ^{−1}-part. Also χ^2 ≠ 1 on H_0: since N is odd, χ^2 = 1 would force all the a_j to be congruent mod N, but the a_j take both values 0 and 1. Symplecticity of γ_1 on the whole of H^{N−2} constrains only the pair of χ- and χ^{−1}-parts, and gives no information on det ρ_{t′}(γ_1). There is no alternative self-pairing either. Lemma 3.1 with α = −1 gives {−b_j} ≠ {b_j}, so the eigenvalues of ρ_{t′}(γ_0) are not closed under inversion. Hence the monodromy on V′_B, which is irreducible because no b_j is 0, preserves no nonzero bilinear form. Avoiding such self-duality is the stated purpose of the choice of the a_j (p. 1255). So the step the "same" proof relies on is not available.

I also looked for another reading and found none. The paper never computes det ρ_{t′}(γ_1), and it never uses the odd-dimensional form of the Picard–Lefschetz formula. Lemma 3.4 shows ρ(γ_1) = BA^{−1} with corner entry C_n, but C_n is not identified with 1. The remark det(γ_1) = 1 on p. 1260 is stated after the lemma and without proof. The needed facts are easy to supply: I checked that b_1 + ⋯ + b_n ≡ 0 mod N from the printed a_j for all n from 3 to 29 and many admissible N, and this also matches the printed list of the b_j. So the statement of Lemma 3.3(3) is correct and only its proof is incomplete.

Unipotence is really used later:
- Lemma 3.7 needs the residual image to be generated by transvections, which is the hypothesis of the classification theorem in [18].
- p. 1260 uses det(γ_1) = 1.
Lemma 3.4 and the irreducibility argument after Definition 3.6 need only rank(ρ_{t′}(γ_1) − 1) = 1.

sourceIssues.reason:
The step fails under the paper's own conventions. The additive character ψ takes values in the p-th roots of unity in Q̄_l (p. 1262). The primes l and p are distinct and prime to N, so ℚ_l(ζ_N, ζ_p) is unramified over ℚ_l. Every σ ∈ G_{ℚ_l} therefore acts on it as a Frobenius power Frob_l^m (m ∈ Ẑ), sending ζ_N to ζ_N^{l^m} and ζ_p to ζ_p^{l^m}.

Let r be the order of l mod N. An element of G_{ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+} sending ζ_N to ζ_N^{−1} exists only when −1 is a power of l mod N, that is, when l^{r/2} ≡ −1 mod N; it then has m ≡ r/2 mod r. The extra condition σ(ζ_p) = ζ_p requires m ≡ 0 modulo the order s of l mod p. Both hold for some m exactly when gcd(r, s) divides r/2, i.e. when v_2(s) < v_2(r). This fails for a positive proportion of primes p.

Two concrete cases satisfy the §3 hypotheses for n = 2 (p. 1259: l an odd prime, N odd and prime to 2l, N > 300):
- N = 307, l = 613 = 2N − 1, p = 5. Here l ≡ −1 mod N forces m to be odd, while 613 ≡ 3 mod 5 has order 4, which forces 4 | m.
- N = 301, l = 3, p = 5. Here 3 has order 42 mod 301 and 3^{21} ≡ −1 mod 301, so m ≡ 21 mod 42 is odd, while 3 has order 4 mod 5.

A direct search of the relevant finite cyclic Galois groups confirms that no σ exists in either case. So (3.3) as printed is not established for the places v above such p. The second line of (3.3) uses σ(ζ_p) = ζ_p essentially, since it leaves ψ(x) unchanged.

When −1 is not a power of l mod N, ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+ = ℚ_l(ζ_N). Then no element of G_{ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+} sends ζ_N to ζ_N^{−1}, so the requested σ does not exist either, but the n = 2 claim is already (3.2).

Defences considered:
- Reading ℚ_l as ℚ throughout the passage would make every step correct (third route). But the paper uses ℚ_l(ζ_N) consistently, in (3.2) and in the statement to be shown, together with Q̄_l-valued ψ, so this is not a slip in one symbol.
- The conclusion does follow from the identity g(v,a)g(v,−a) = q printed a few lines earlier, since b_2 = −b_1. The paper never draws this conclusion, however; it rests the n = 2 case on the nonexistent σ.

Hence the step is wrong but locally repairable. The asserted membership is true, since the product equals q. A numerical check of g(v,(N−1)/2)g(v,(N+1)/2) = q for (N, q) = (11, 23), (15, 31) and (307, 1229) agrees.

Reach: Lemma 3.9 stands, and so do the main results. At both primes where §4 applies the lemma, −1 is not a power of the prime mod N: l satisfies N ∤ l^{r/2} + 1 (p. 1268), and l′ ≡ 1 mod N (Proposition 4.1). There ℚ_l(ζ_N)^+ = ℚ_l(ζ_N), so (3.2) suffices. arXiv:2104.09761v1, p. 18, has the same sentence.

sourceIssues.locator: Remark 3.13, p. 1268
sourceIssues.printed: The source attributes to the proof of [14] the assertion that v(t) < 0 makes V_{λ,t} semistable as a G_{F_v}-representation, with maximally nilpotent N in its Weil-Deligne representation.
sourceIssues.correction: Claim only what the proof in [14] gives. Take t ∈ F_v with v(t) = −d < 0 and write t^{−1} = uπ^d, where u is a unit and π is a uniformiser. Then V_{λ,t} is potentially semistable. It becomes semistable on restriction to G_{F′}, where F′ = F_v(π^{1/e}) is the totally ramified extension of [14, Theorem 1.4]. The integer e comes from a toroidal subdivision and is not controlled. The rest of the sentence holds as printed: the monodromy operator N of WD(V_{λ,t}) can be computed from D_st over F′, and it is maximally nilpotent. The argument of [14] gives semistability over F_v itself only when v(t) = −1. In that case the blow-up of [14, Lemma 2.1], base-changed along T ↦ t^{−1}, is already a semistable model of Y_t over O_{F_v}. For v(t) ≤ −2 the claim needs a separate argument. One option is a semistable model of Y_t over O_{F_v}; this means gluing compatible semistable resolutions of the local models uπ^d = Z_1⋯Z_r. Another is to combine two facts: ℓ′-adic inertia acts unipotently on the whole middle cohomology, as in the proof of Lemma 3.12, and the traces of inertia on D_pst do not depend on ℓ, by Ochiai's theorem.
sourceIssues.reason:
The remark cites the proof of the main theorem of [14]. That proof works throughout over an auxiliary ramified extension:
- Theorem 1.4 and Theorem 2.3 of [14] (arXiv:2103.00106v1, pp. 3 and 9) give a semistable model of the Dwork hypersurface only over O_{F′}, where F′ = F(π^{1/e}).
- The integer e comes from the subdivision theorem of Kempf, Knudsen, Mumford and Saint-Donat (pp. 11–12), and it is never shown to be 1.
- Only the case of valuation −1 is settled over F itself (p. 8, after Remark 2.2). The same page notes that the naive base change for d ≥ 2 has local form uπ^d = Z_1⋯Z_r, which is not semistable.
- Section 4 of [14] (p. 19) reduces at the start to proving that V_{λ,t^{−1}} is regular and ordinary as a G_{F′}-representation. The operator N is then computed on D_st over F′, using Tsuji's comparison theorem for the model over O_{F′} (pp. 20–21).
- Lemma 4.1 of [14] descends from F′ to F only the properties de Rham, regular and ordinary, never semistability.
- The main theorem of [14] is itself stated for an arbitrary finite extension F_0, and its proof replaces F_0 by F′.

Attempts to defend the text:
1. Read "semistable" as "potentially semistable". This would make the sentence correct, but the paper keeps the two notions apart: its Theorem 1.4 (p. 1241) requires r|_{G_{F_v}} to be "potentially semistable". The remark also offers its claim as the p-adic analogue of the unipotent ℓ′-adic inertia of Lemma 3.12, which points to genuine semistability. So the missing word is not a plain misprint.
2. Look for the claim elsewhere in the paper. Nothing supplies it. Remark 4.4 proves only ordinarity, via local–global compatibility, and ordinarity in the sense of [1] does not imply semistability over F_v.

The statement about N is correct. The Weil–Deligne representation of a potentially semistable representation can be computed from D_st over any extension over which it becomes semistable. F′/F_v is totally ramified, so the maximal unramified subfield is unchanged, and [14] shows N is maximally nilpotent on each embedding component. The semistability claim is plausible, but the cited proof does not establish it.

Nothing depends on the remark. It says itself that the result of [14] is not needed. The main proof uses the ℓ′-adic Lemma 3.12, through Lemma 4.3, and Remark 4.4 refers back to Remark 3.13 only for ordinarity. The remark does not appear in arXiv v1. There, Lemma 3.10(4) cited [14] only for "regular and ordinary". The published paper is the final version, and arXiv has no later version of either paper.

For example, ℚ(√2) and ℚ(√3) each meet ℚ(√6) only in ℚ, but their composite contains √6. sourceIssues.locator: Definition 4.4.1 and Proposition 4.4.2, pp. 41–42
sourceIssues.printed: Item 2 specifies, for i = 1, 2, isomorphisms η_i : ∧^n W̄_{λ_i} → ∧^n Ū_{λ_i,T_{0,F}}. The functor F({Ū_{λ_i}}) has a representing scheme T({Ū_{λ_i}}), finite étale over T_{0,F}. Proposition 4.4.2 asserts that T({Ū_{λ_i}}) is smooth over F and geometrically irreducible.
sourceIssues.correction: In the unitary case require η_i to be compatible with the forms induced by the pairings on ∧^n (such η_i exist, since the norm 𝔽_{l²}^× → 𝔽_l^× is surjective), or state Proposition 4.4.2 for T nonempty.
sourceIssues.reason: When −1 mod N ∈ ⟨l_i⟩ the functor asks for isometries φ_i with ∧^nφ_i = η_i; the values of ∧^nφ over all isometries form a coset of the norm-one elements, so if η_i is not compatible with the induced forms the scheme is empty (replacing ⟨,⟩_U by −⟨,⟩_U rescales the ∧^n form by (−1)^n). An empty scheme is not geometrically irreducible. The nonemptiness claim on p. 60 appeals only to the uniqueness of Hermitian spaces, which does not address η.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Proposition 4.2.5(1), p. 38
sourceIssues.printed: The proof invokes [KM74, Theorem 2(2)] to place the coefficients in O_M for the characteristic polynomial on this group of each h·Frob_v, h ∈ H. It then infers that Q_v(X) has coefficients in O_M[X].
sourceIssues.correction: Integrality of Q_v does not follow, since Q_v is computed on W = V ⊗ Ψ_λ^{−1} and Ψ(ϖ_v) is not a unit at primes above char v. It holds instead because W_{t,λ} is an O_{M_λ}-lattice for every λ ∤ char v with Q_v independent of λ, and at char v by crystallinity with non-negative Hodge–Tate weights.
sourceIssues.reason: Twisting by the non-unit Ψ(Frob_v)^{−1} can destroy integrality at primes above char v.

sourceIssues.locator: Proposition 6.2.3(13), p. 55, and the proof of Theorem 6.2.4, pp. 59–60
sourceIssues.printed: For m > 2, the proposition asserts that r̄_{aux,𝔭}(G_F) is conjugate to GU_m(𝔽_{p²}), with ε̄^{1−m} as the multiplier character of r̄_{aux,𝔭}. The proof uses a homomorphism π_1^ét(T_{F_4}) → GU_m(𝔽_{p²}) and asserts r̄_{aux,𝔭}(G_{F_5}) = GU_m(𝔽_{p²}).
sourceIssues.correction: Require r̄_{aux,𝔭} to take values in GU_m(𝔽_{p²}) with multiplier ε̄^{1−m} and r̄_{aux,𝔭}(G_{F(ζ_p)}) = SU_m(𝔽_{p²}), which is all Lemma 5.2.4 uses; in Theorem 6.2.4 take f onto its image G ⊇ SU_m(𝔽_{p²}) (the geometric monodromy of Proposition 4.4.2).
sourceIssues.reason: (8b) requires det r_{aux,λ} = ε^{−m(m−1)/2}, so det r̄_{aux,𝔭} takes values in 𝔽_p^×; but GU_m(𝔽_{p²}) contains diag(u, 1, …, 1) with u^{p+1} = 1 and u ≠ ±1, whose determinant is not in 𝔽_p^×. So the hypotheses of Proposition 6.2.3 are inconsistent for m > 2 as printed, and the proof of Theorem 6.2.4 asserts a false image.

sourceIssues.locator: §4, definition of the cover T_W, p. 27 (author copy; p. 54 of the published version)
sourceIssues.printed: T_W is defined as the scheme of all isomorphisms W_S ≅ V[𝔫]((N − 1 − n)/2)_S, with no condition on the alternating pairings.
sourceIssues.correction: The isomorphisms must be compatible with the symplectic structures; only then is T_W a torsor under the symplectic group and geometrically connected by Proposition 4.2.
sourceIssues.reason: Without the condition the fibre is a torsor under GL_n(𝒪/𝔫) on which the symplectic geometric monodromy acts with many orbits, so the scheme is not geometrically connected.

restructure.detail: The design brief asked this roadmap to build Qian's Lemma 2.1 (n-th roots of finite-field-valued characters after a totally real base change avoiding a given field, with its obstruction and two-primary steps). The accepted ArithmeticGaloisDuality packet already plans it: R02.4/character-root-obstruction (citing the proof of Qian's Lemma 2.1, pp. 1245–1247) and R02.4/character-roots-after-base-change (m-th roots of finite-order characters of a CM field after a totally real Galois extension disjoint from a given field), with R02.4/all-place-sha-duality for the Poitou–Tate step.
restructure.proposal: ArithmeticGaloisDuality R02.4 owns Lemma 2.1. This roadmap imports it in DM.6/determinant-matching-at-l, DM.6/determinant-matching-at-auxiliary-prime and DM.9/switching-determinant-data, after reducing (k^×)^n-valued characters to the prime-to-l exponent m and identifying k^× with μ_{#k−1} by Teichmüller lifting. No node of this roadmap plans the root extraction.

restructure.detail: Companion matrices are planned in the accepted ClassicalArithmeticCompletion packet (CA.2/companion-matrix with characteristic and minimal polynomial), in the same orientation as Qian Lemma 3.4 and BLGHT11 Corollary 4.4.
restructure.proposal: ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.2 owns the companion matrix. This roadmap adds only DM.0/companion-normal-form (cyclic vectors, the single Jordan block of C((X − 1)^n), and the rank-one property of C(q)C(p)^{−1} − 1), which no layer of CA.2 states, and Levelt's theorem.

restructure.detail: The extraction of Boxer–Calegari–Gee–Newton–Thorne routes their Lemma 5.2.3 (perfectness of SL_n and SU_n over finite fields, simplicity of PSL_n and PSU_n, non-isomorphism across characteristics) to ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations R01.4/G7 as a source, but the accepted packets of that roadmap plan only the rank-two case (R01.4/normal-subgroups-and-automorphisms-of-psl2-pgl2). Qian's extraction places the same facts (its items 125–126) with the Dwork family, whose Lemma 3.7 and Proposition 3.8 use them.
restructure.proposal: This roadmap owns, in DM.0, the normal subgroups of SL_n and SU_n and simplicity of PSL_n and PSU_n over finite fields of odd characteristic (DM.0/special-linear-unitary-simple), Artin's non-isomorphism theorem (DM.0/artin-non-isomorphism) and the Zalesskii–Serezhkin classification for n > 2 (DM.0/zalesskii-serezhkin-classification). ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations G7, and BCGNT25's Lemmas 5.2.4–5.2.6 wherever they are planned, import them from DM.0. If the maintainer later creates a roadmap for finite groups of Lie type, these three nodes move there unchanged.
